generatedProse.concept-context: In psychology, searching is rarely a quick lookup. When you look for evidence on a topic such as sleep and memory, you are exploring a question the field is still arguing over, not fetching one fact. You try some terms, see what the literature returns, and search again with better ones. Treating a search this way, as exploratory, iterative and planned, is what finding sources for psychology asks of you.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two psychology students given the same essay question and told to find sources for it.

Tom types the whole essay question into a search box, glances at the first few results, and picks the one at the top. The search is over in a minute. But Tom has treated this like looking up a fact: one attempt, no plan, and whatever came first. There was no sense of what a good psychology source would look like or how to look again. This is everyday searching.

Amara starts by asking what the question is really about and what sort of study would answer it. She tries a few terms, sees what the literature returns, and searches again with better words when the first set is too broad. Her search takes longer, but it is exploratory, iterative and planned. This is academic searching.

Both students searched. Only Amara treated searching as a discipline rather than a quick lookup.
generatedProse.summary: Academic searching in psychology is more than looking something up. It is exploratory, because you are following a question the field still debates; iterative, because you search again with better words; and strategy-driven, because you plan before you start. You can now explain what academic searching is and tell it apart from the everyday searching you already do. The next lesson looks at what makes a search effective.

check.body: In the worked example, what made Amara's approach academic rather than everyday?

items.text: She planned what she wanted, tried some terms, and searched again with better ones.
She finished the search more quickly than Tom did.
She typed the whole essay question into the search box.
She picked the result at the top of the list.

feedback.correct: That's right. Planning, trying terms and searching again is academic searching in action.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what Amara DID differently, beyond finishing fast or taking the first result.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara was academic because she planned, tried terms and searched again. Finishing fast, typing the whole question or taking the top result are all the everyday approach.
